source_text: Περὶ μὲν τοῦ γνωστικοῦ τοσαῦτα ὡς ἐν ἐπιδρομῇ, χωρῶμεν δὲ ἤδη ἐπὶ τὰ ἑξῆς, καὶ δὴ τὴν πίστιν αὖθις διαθρητέον· εἰσὶ γὰρ οἱ τὴν μὲν πίστιν ἡμῶν περὶ περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ, τὴν δὲ γνῶσιν περὶ τοῦ πατρὸς εἶναι διαστέλλοντες. λέληθεν δὲ αὐτοὺς ὅτι πιστεῦσαι μὲν ἀληθῶς τῷ υἱῷ δεῖ, ὅτι τε υἱὸς καὶ ὅτι ἦλθεν καὶ πῶς καὶ διὰ τί καὶ περὶ τοῦ πάθους, γνῶναι δὲ ἀνάγκη τίς ἐστὶν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ. ἤδη δὲ οὔτε ἡ γνῶσις ἄνευ πίστεως οὔθ’ ἡ πίστις ἄνευ γνώσεως, οὐ μὴν οὐδὲ ὁ πατὴρ ἄνευ υἱοῦ· ἅμα γὰρ τῷ πατὴρ υἱοῦ πατήρ, υἱὸς δὲ περὶ πατρὸς ἀληθὴς διδάσκαλος. καὶ ἵνα τις πιστεύσῃ τῷ υἱῷ, γνῶναι δεῖ τὸν πατέρα πρὸς ὃν καὶ ὁ υἱός. αὖθίς τε ἵνα τὸν πατέρα ἐπιγνῶμεν, πιστεῦσαι δεῖ τῷ υἱῷ, ὅτι ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ υἱὸς διδάσκει· ἐκ πίστεως γὰρ εἰς γνῶσιν, διὰ υἱοῦ πατήρ· γνῶσις δὲ υἱοῦ καὶ πατρὸς ἡ κατὰ τὸν κανόνα τὸν γνωστικὸν τὸν τῷ ὄντι γνωστικὸν ἐπιβολὴ καὶ διάληψίς ἐστιν ἀληθείας διὰ τῆς ἀληθείας. ἡμεῖς ἄρα ἐσμὲν οἱ ἐν τῷ ἀπιστουμένῳ πιστοὶ καὶ οἱ ἐν τῷ ἀγνώστῳ γνωστικοί, τουτέστιν ἐν τῷ πᾶσιν ἀγνοουμένῳ καὶ ἀπιστουμένῳ, ὀλίγοις δὲ πιστευομένῳ τε καὶ γινωσκομένῳ γνωστικοί· γνωστικοὶ δὲ οὐ λόγῳ, ἔργα ἀπογραφόμενοι, ἀλλ’ αὐτῇ τῇ θεωρίᾳ. Μακάριος ὁ λέγων εἰς ὦτα ἀκουόντων· πίστις δὲ ὦτα ψυχῆς, καὶ ταύτην αἰνίσσεται τὴν πίστιν ὁ κύριος λέγων ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκούειν ἀκουέτω, ἵνα δὴ πιστεύσας συνῇ ἃ λέγει, ὡς λέγει. ἀλλά τοι καὶ Ὅμηρος ὁ ποιητῶν πρεσβύτατος ἐπὶ τοῦ αἰσθάνεσθαι τῷ ἀκούειν, εἰδικῷ ἀντὶ γενικοῦ, χρησάμενος μάλιστα δέ τ’ ἔκλυον αὐτοὶ γράφει· τὸ γὰρ ὅλον ἡ συνῳδία καὶ ἡ συμφωνία τῆς ἀμφοῖν πίστεως εἰς ἓν πέρας καταγίνεται τὴν σωτηρίαν. μάρτυς ἡμῖν νημερτὴς ὁ ἀπόστολος λέγων· ἐπιποθῶ γὰρ ἰδεῖν ὑμᾶς, ἵνα τι μεταδῶ χάρισμα ὑμῖν πνευματικὸν εἰς τὸ στηριχθῆναι ὑμᾶς· τοῦτο δέ ἐστι συμπαρακληθῆναι ἐν ὑμῖν διὰ τῆς ἐν ἀλλήλοις πίστεως ὑμῶν τε καὶ ἐμοῦ. καὶ πάλιν ὑποβὰς ἐπάγει· δικαιοσύνη δὲ θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ ἀποκαλύπτεται ἐκ πίστεως εἰς πίστιν. φαίνεται οὖν ὁ ἀπόστολος διττὴν καταγγέλλων πίστιν, μᾶλλον δὲ μίαν, αὔξησιν καὶ τελείωσιν ἐπιδεχομένην· ἡ μὲν γὰρ κοινὴ πίστις καθάπερ θεμέλιος ὑπόκειται (τοῖς γοῦν θεραπευθῆναι ποθοῦσιν ὁ κύριος πιστῶς κινουμένοις ἐπέλεγεν· ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε·), ἡ δὲ ἐξαίρετος ἐποικοδομουμένη συντελειοῦται τῷ πιστῷ καὶ συναπαρτίζεται αὖ τῇ ἐκ μαθήσεως περιγινομένῃ καὶ τοῦ λόγου τὰς ἐντολὰς ἐπιτελεῖν, ὁποῖοι ἦσαν οἱ ἀπόστολοι, ἐφ’ ὧν τὴν πίστιν ὄρη μετατιθέναι καὶ δένδρα μεταφυτεύειν δύνασθαι εἴρηται.
pass_a_gloss: Concerning the gnosis, we have said enough in passing; let us proceed to what follows, and again, we must thoroughly examine faith; for there are those who distinguish our faith concerning the Son from the knowledge concerning the Father. It has escaped them that one must truly believe in the Son, both that He is the Son and that He came, and how and why, and concerning His passion; but it is necessary to know who the Son of God is. Now, neither is knowledge without faith, nor faith without knowledge, nor the Father without the Son; for the Father is the Father of the Son, and the Son is the true teacher concerning the Father. And in order that one may believe in the Son, it is necessary to know the Father, towards whom also the Son is; and again, in order that we may know the Father, it is necessary to believe in the Son, because the Son of God teaches; for from faith to knowledge, through the Son, is the Father; and knowledge of the Son and the Father is the contemplation and apprehension of truth through truth. We, therefore, are those who are faithful in what is not believed and knowledgeable in what is not known, that is, in what is unknown and not believed by all, but believed and known by a few; and we are knowledgeable not in word, but in deeds, and in the very contemplation itself. Blessed is he who says to those who listen; faith is the ears of the soul, and the Lord praises this faith, saying, 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear,' so that, having believed, he may understand what is said, as it is said. But also Homer, the oldest of poets, using the specific instead of the general, writes that they heard with their own ears; for the whole is the harmony and symphony of the two faiths, leading to one end, salvation. The Apostle is a true witness to us, saying, 'I long to see you, that I may impart some spiritual gift to you, to strengthen you; this is to be comforted together among you through the faith that is in each other, yours and mine.' And again, he adds, 'The righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith.' The Apostle, therefore, seems to proclaim a twofold faith, or rather one faith that admits of increase and perfection; for the common faith, like a foundation, is laid (for the Lord said to those who were healed, 'Your faith has saved you'), and the extraordinary faith is built upon and perfected with the faithful, and is again equipped with the knowledge that comes from teaching and the commands of the Word, such as the Apostles were, concerning whom it is said that they could move mountains and transplant trees through faith.

bible_refs.note: The righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith

pass_b_english: We have said enough about the gnosis in passing, so let us now move on to what comes next, and we must once again examine faith thoroughly. For there are people who distinguish our faith concerning the Son from knowledge concerning the Father. They have missed the fact that one must truly believe in the Son—that He is the Son, that He came, and how and why He came, and concerning His passion—yet it is necessary to know who the Son of God is. Now neither knowledge without faith nor faith without knowledge exists, nor the Father without the Son; for the Father is the Father of the Son, and the Son is the true teacher concerning the Father. And in order that one may believe in the Son, it is necessary to know the Father, toward whom the Son also is; and again, in order that we may know the Father, it is necessary to believe in the Son, because the Son of God teaches. For from faith to knowledge, through the Son, comes the Father; and knowledge of the Son and the Father is the contemplation and apprehension of truth through truth.

Therefore we are the ones who are faithful in what is not believed and knowledgeable in what is not known—that is, in what is unknown and not believed by all, but believed and known by a few. And we are knowledgeable not in word, by recording deeds, but in the very contemplation itself. Blessed is the one who speaks to those who listen; faith is the ears of the soul, and the Lord praises this faith by saying, 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear' (Matt. 11:15), so that, having believed, he may understand what is said, just as it is said. But Homer also, the oldest of the poets, using the specific for the general when he writes of perceiving by hearing, writes most especially that they heard with their own ears; for the whole harmony and symphony of the two faiths leads to one end, salvation. The Apostle is a true witness to us, saying, 'I long to see you, that I may impart some spiritual gift to you to strengthen you—that is, that we may be mutually encouraged by each other's faith, both yours and mine' (Rom. 1:11–12). And again he adds, 'The righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith' (Rom. 1:17). The Apostle, therefore, appears to proclaim a twofold faith, or rather one faith that admits of increase and perfection. For the common faith lies like a foundation (for the Lord said to those who were healed, 'Your faith has saved you' [Matt. 9:22]), and the extraordinary faith is built up and perfected with the faithful, and is again equipped with the knowledge that comes from teaching and with fulfilling the commands of the Word—such as the Apostles were, concerning whom it is said that they could move mountains and transplant trees through faith (Matt. 17:20).
